q: What is the joinery of Figure B that is formed by overlapping two pieces of material, providing a simple and strong joint?
n: A lap joint overlaps the two pieces, usually with each cut to half thickness (half-lap), and fastens them face to face, giving a simple, strong joint. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (wood joinery).

q: What is the joinery of Figure C that is a rectangular slot cut across the grain of a board to receive the end of another board, often used in shelving?
n: A dado is a rectangular groove cut across the grain of a board to receive the end of another board. It is the classic joint for fixed shelves. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (wood joinery).

q: What is the joinery of Figure D that is an L-shaped cut along the edge or end of a board to allow another piece to fit into it, commonly used in cabinet and casework construction?
n: A rabbet is an L-shaped cut along the edge or end of a board that receives another piece. It is used for cabinet backs and casework corners. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (wood joinery).

q: What is the joinery of Figure E that is an interlocking joint with fan-shaped pins and tails, known for its strength and decorative appearance, often used in drawer construction?
n: A dovetail joint interlocks fan-shaped pins and tails that resist being pulled apart. It is the traditional strong, decorative drawer joint. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (wood joinery).

q: Identify Figure A that is the inclined structural support on the inner side of a staircase, often located next to a wall.
n: The inner (wall) string is the inclined board on the wall side of a stair that carries the ends of the treads and risers. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture (stairs).

q: Identify Figure B that is the decorative and widened end of the lowest step, often used with a volute handrail.
n: The curtail step is the bottom step, widened with a rounded or scrolled end that receives the volute of the handrail. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture (stairs).

q: Identify Figure C that is the vertical member supporting the handrail, spaced evenly along the length of a staircase.
n: Balusters are the evenly spaced vertical members between the treads or string and the handrail, supporting the rail and closing the open side. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture (stairs).

q: Identify Figure D that is the large vertical post at the start or end of a flight of stairs, anchoring the handrail.
n: The newel post is the large post at the start, end or turn of a flight that anchors the handrail and strings. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture (stairs).

q: Identify Figure E that is a horizontal platform between two flights of stairs, used for resting or changing direction.
n: A landing is the horizontal platform between flights, used for rest or to change direction. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture; NBC IRR Rule XII (stair landings).

q: Identify Figure A that is a method of edge joining where one board has a protruding ridge and the other a matching groove, creating a tight interlock.
n: Tongue-and-groove (T&G) boards have a ridge on one edge and a matching groove on the other, so the boards interlock tightly. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (wood joinery).

q: Identify Figure B that is a thin strip inserted into matching grooves along the edges of boards, aligning and strengthening the joint?
n: A spline is a thin strip glued into matching grooves cut in both edges, aligning and strengthening the joint. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (wood joinery).

q: Identify Figure C that is a basic end-to-end wood joint with square cuts, commonly used when lengthening members.
n: A square splice joins two members end to end with square-cut ends (usually with side plates), the basic way of lengthening a timber. Source: Timber construction references (e.g., Breyer, Design of Wood Structures).

q: Identify Figure D, a joint where two members meet end to end and are held by bolted side plates.
n: A fish joint butts two members end to end and clamps them between bolted side plates (fish plates). Source: Timber construction references; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Identify Figure E that is a wood joint made by interlocking a series of rectangular “fingers” to provide high tensile strength and gluing surface.
n: A finger joint interlocks a series of rectangular fingers, giving a large glue area and high tensile strength. It is used to make long lengths from short pieces. Source: ASTM D5572 (finger joints); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Which woodworking equipment is a jigsaw?
n: Figure A is the jigsaw, a handheld saw with a thin reciprocating blade for curved cuts. Source: Power tool manufacturer literature.

q: Which woodworking equipment is a bench drill press?
n: Figure C is the bench drill press, a drill mounted on a column over a table for accurate vertical holes. Source: Power tool manufacturer literature.

q: Which woodworking equipment is a belt sander?
n: Figure B is the belt sander, which uses a continuous abrasive belt for fast stock removal. Source: Power tool manufacturer literature.

q: Which woodworking equipment is a circular saw?
n: Figure E is the circular saw, which has a rotating toothed disc blade for straight cuts. Source: Power tool manufacturer literature.

q: Which woodworking equipment is a router?
n: Figure D is the router, a high-speed spindle tool for cutting profiles, grooves and edges. Source: Power tool manufacturer literature.

q: The actual (dressed) width of solid lumber is less than its nominal size by about how many millimeters?
n: Lumber is named by its rough (nominal) size. Planing (dressing) removes about 1/2" (about 12 mm), so a nominal 2" × 4" is actually about 1-1/2" × 3-1/2". Source: US Forest Service, Wood Handbook; PS 20 American Softwood Lumber Standard.

q: For preliminary design, what is the recommended maximum span of a solid wood beam?
n: For preliminary design, solid sawn wood beams are economical up to spans of about 3 m. Longer spans call for glulam, trusses or steel. Source: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated (span ranges).

q: Which wood is known as Philippine ebony?
n: Kamagong (Diospyros blancoi) is the native Philippine ebony, a very dense, dark heartwood prized for furniture and carving. Source: DENR-FPRDI, Philippine timber species references.

q: In the Philippines, lumber is commonly sold in what lengths?
n: In the Philippines, lumber is sold in even-foot lengths: 8', 10', 12' and so on. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (lumber).

q: Which of these is also called chipboard?
n: Chipboard is another name for particle board: wood chips and particles bonded with resin and pressed into panels. Source: ANSI A208.1 (particleboard).

q: What are the wooden strips laid on a concrete slab to fasten a subfloor or wood flooring to?
n: Sleepers are wood strips laid on and anchored to a concrete slab. They give a nailing base for the subfloor or wood flooring and an air space. Source: NWFA Installation Guidelines; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What protects engineered wood from moisture?
n: A foam underlayment under floating engineered wood acts as a moisture barrier and cushion between the slab and the boards. Source: NWFA Installation Guidelines; flooring manufacturer literature.

q: What is laid on the slab before installing wood flooring?
n: Sleepers are first fixed on the concrete slab to carry and nail the wood flooring. Source: NWFA Installation Guidelines; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What does S2S stand for in lumber?
n: S2S means surfaced two sides: lumber planed smooth on two faces (S4S is planed on all four). Source: PS 20 American Softwood Lumber Standard; US Forest Service, Wood Handbook.

q: What is the heavy horizontal timber at the bottom of a wood frame, resting on the foundation?
n: The sill plate is the horizontal timber anchored on the foundation wall that receives the floor joists or studs. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (wood light framing).

q: Which of the following is classified as a softwood?
n: Benguet pine (Pinus kesiya) is a conifer, hence a softwood. Tanguile, yakal and molave are broadleaf hardwoods. Source: DENR-FPRDI timber species references.

q: Conifers are classified as what kind of wood?
n: Conifers (cone-bearing trees such as pine and fir) are botanically softwoods, whatever their actual hardness. Source: US Forest Service, Wood Handbook.

q: Which wood is known as Philippine mahogany?
n: Tanguile and other lauan (Shorea) species are traded internationally as Philippine mahogany. Source: DENR-FPRDI timber species references; US Forest Service, Wood Handbook.

q: Which wood is commonly used for door frames for its strength and durability?
n: Yakal (Shorea astylosa) is a very dense, durable hardwood used for door frames, posts and structural members. Source: DENR-FPRDI timber species references.

q: Which native Philippine tree is known for its dense, durable hardwood?
n: Narra (Pterocarpus indicus), the national tree, is a native dense and durable hardwood. Mahogany, acacia and pine are introduced species. Source: DENR-FPRDI timber species references.

q: What is undressed lumber called?
n: Rough lumber is lumber as sawn, not yet dressed (planed). Source: US Forest Service, Wood Handbook; Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate.
